analysis.one_liner: Loosens a range of post-2008 bank and market rules, framed as relief for small companies.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 320-102 on September 16, 2014, but the Senate Banking Committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill packaged eleven changes to the Dodd-Frank financial rules into one bill. Some provisions genuinely cut paperwork for small and young companies trying to raise money, like simpler disclosure forms and a registration exemption for brokers who help sell small private companies. Others roll back core parts of the post-2008 Wall Street overhaul: banks and derivatives dealers would face no minimum margin (collateral) requirements on certain unverified swap deals, banks could keep holding bundles of corporate loans that the Volcker Rule would otherwise force them to shed, and advisers to small-business investment funds would be exempt from both SEC and state registration. The House passed it with a strong bipartisan vote, but the Senate took no action.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks and derivatives dealers benefit from margin exemptions and relief from the Volcker Rule's requirement to divest certain collateralized loan obligations. Private fund and venture capital advisers benefit from exemption from SEC and state registration. Small and emerging companies benefit from lighter disclosure requirements, and merger-and-acquisition brokers get a registration exemption. Non-financial companies hedging business risk also avoid posting margin on their uncleared swaps.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks, derivatives dealers, private fund advisers, small issuers

how_it_helps.text: Exempts swaps between swap dealers and non-financial companies that hedge commercial risk — plus certain cooperative and affiliate arrangements — from prudential regulators' initial and variation margin requirements for uncleared swaps, so hedgers do not have to post collateral [S2] [S3] [S4].

Blocks the Volcker Rule (the ban on banks' proprietary trading) from forcing banks to divest debt securities of pre-existing collateralized loan obligations before July 2017, and says holding such debt alone is not an 'ownership interest' [S2] [S4].
Exempts advisers to small business investment companies from SEC registration and reporting requirements and from parallel state or local registration laws [S2] [S4].

Exempts merger and acquisition brokers who facilitate sales of small private companies (under roughly $250 million revenue) from broker-dealer registration, with guardrails for those handling customer funds or public offerings [S2] [S4].

Exempts emerging growth companies and issuers with under $250 million in revenue from the XBRL machine-readable reporting requirement, and directs the SEC to simplify and scale disclosure rules for smaller issuers [S2] [S3] [S4].

Establishes a pilot program quoting small-company stocks in wider price increments and lets young companies file IPO registration drafts confidentially earlier, to reduce costs and encourage trading in small-cap stocks [S2] [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Margin and disclosure exemptions shift risk and information costs onto the broader market: less collateral backs unverified swap deals, banks keep holdings the Volcker Rule was meant to curb, investors get less machine-readable company data, and private fund advisers escape state-level oversight. If riskier positions fail, the costs of a bailout fall on taxpayers and depositors.
analysis.who_pays_short: Investors and anyone exposed to market risk

drawbacks.text: Exempting uncleared swaps from margin requirements means less collateral backs these deals; margin requirements exist because uncollateralized derivatives amplified losses in the 2008 crisis [S2] [S3] [S4].

The Volcker Rule relief lets banks retain investments in collateralized loan obligations — bundles of corporate loans — that the rule otherwise required them to divest, keeping bank capital exposed to loan-market losses [S2] [S4].
The SBIC adviser exemption applies to state and local registration and licensing laws too, removing a layer of state-level oversight of investment advisers [S2] [S4].

Raising the disclosure threshold for employee stock benefit plans from $5 million to $10 million means investors receive less information about how company shares sold under employee compensation plans are priced [S2] [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The paperwork relief for genuinely small companies — simpler disclosure, an M&A broker exemption with real guardrails, a small-cap trading pilot — is modest but legitimate, and supporters argued Dodd-Frank rules were written with big banks in mind and hit small firms hardest. The serious trade-off sits in the provisions aimed at large institutions: exempting uncleared swaps from margin, keeping banks in CLOs, and stripping state oversight of certain advisers all chip away at the post-2008 safety rules without the issue having gone through a regulatory cost-benefit process. Whether that trade was worth it was never tested in the Senate.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a fast-track vote requiring two-thirds approval, but the Senate referred it to its Banking Committee, which never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The House considered the bill under 'suspension of the rules' — a fast-track procedure that allows passage without amendments but requires a two-thirds vote — on September 15-16, 2014 [S6] [S7].
On September 16, 2014, the House passed it 320-102: 225 of 232 Republicans and 95 of 199 Democrats voted yes [S7].
The Senate received the bill on September 17, 2014, read it twice, and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, where no further action was taken [S6] [S4].
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, so the bill died in committee without a Senate vote [S1] [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Dodd-Frank safeguards the bill would have loosened stayed in place for the moment, so investors and anyone counting on post-2008 derivatives and banking rules were better off that it died. Banks and private fund advisers lost a legislative route to relief, though regulators later addressed some of the same issues on their own.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Post-2008 financial safeguards, and the investors relying on them

sides.party_line_note: Republicans were nearly unanimous (225-1), while Democrats split roughly in half, 95 for and 101 against, on final passage [S7].

industries.note: The bill exempts their uncleared swaps with commercial counterparties from margin requirements and keeps banks in pre-2014 collateralized loan obligations without triggering Volcker Rule divestiture, reducing the collateral and capital safeguards that backstop the market everyone relies on.

industries.industry: Private equity and venture capital fund advisers
industries.note: Advisers to small business investment companies are exempted from SEC registration and reporting and from state registration laws, removing a layer of oversight over funds that pool other people's money.

XBRL exemption, scaled disclosure rules, earlier confidential IPO filings, and a wider stock-quote pilot cut their compliance costs — but each exemption also means less standardized information for the investors who buy their shares.

Brokers facilitating sales of small private companies are exempt from broker-dealer registration, though brokers handling customer funds or public offerings remain covered; lower costs flow to small business sellers and buyers.

industries.industry: XBRL data and financial reporting software vendors
industries.note: Exempting small issuers from the machine-readable filing mandate shrinks a market that existed only because of the mandate, while investors lose the standardized data the mandate produced.
